meta.blurb: Eight guests cross a tidal causeway to Tern Rock Lodge for a weekend of goodbyes. Then the storm shuts the sea road, the lights go out, and the host is dead at the bottom of the cellar steps. Ines Calloway must find the killer before the tide turns.
meta.bible: Ines Calloway: an insurance investigator in her thirties, calm, observant and stubborn; she comes to value the lodge's paintings and tells the story as it happens. Orla Venn: the seventy-year-old owner of Tern Rock Lodge, sharp and warm; she is selling the lodge; she is found dead in the cellar. Felix Venn: Orla's nephew, charming, in debt; he searches the study at night looking for her new will. Hugh Marlowe: Orla's accountant, nervous; he has been borrowing from her account and plans to repay it. Dr Priya Nair: Orla's doctor and old friend, calm and clear. Gideon Frost: an elderly painter and friend of Orla, grumpy; he painted The Grey Heron and knows its secret, a tiny white fleck in the heron's eye. Lucas Reyes: a smooth art dealer, the buyer's agent; he stole the real painting and killed Orla in the cellar. Tamsin Reed: a young journalist writing about the lodge; she is shut in the cold store. Marta Okoye: Orla's lawyer, who knows the new will: the lodge goes to the island's lifeboat. Mr Bell: the caretaker and boatman, steady and practical; his boat is wrecked in the storm. Mrs Bright: the cook, who notices everything. Tern Rock Lodge: an old stone hotel on a small island, reached by a causeway that floods at high tide. The Grey Heron: the lodge's most valuable painting, hung in the study; the hanging copy has no fleck in the eye. Reyes Fine Art: Lucas's gallery, named on a label found in the cellar. Facts: the cellar door has a bolt on the outside; Orla's watch stopped at 8.58; the lights failed at 9.05; the cellar is at the back, past the kitchen; the cloakroom is at the front; low tide opens the causeway about 4.40 on Sunday morning. Voice and tone: tense, fair and clear, a puzzle told step by step; the death is stated plainly with no gore; every clue is shown to the reader.

B1B2: Mr Bell drives Ines across the stone causeway to Tern Rock Lodge. The tide is low, but dark clouds are already gathering over the sea.
Orla Venn is waiting at the door of the old stone lodge, leaning on a stick. She is seventy years old, but her eyes are bright and quick.
Orla explains that she is going to sell the lodge and its paintings. She has asked Ines, as an insurance investigator, to examine the pictures carefully and to tell her the truth.
Orla leads Ines past a tall grandfather clock to the study. There hangs her best painting, The Grey Heron, which shows a lonely bird at the edge of the sea.
In the lounge Ines meets Felix Venn, Orla's nephew, who is charming and loud. Beside him sits Hugh Marlowe, her accountant, who keeps looking at his watch.
Next Ines meets Dr Priya Nair, who is Orla's doctor and an old friend. Gideon Frost, the painter of The Grey Heron, sits nearby, grumbling about the weather.
The last three guests are Lucas Reyes, a smooth art dealer, Tamsin Reed, a young writer, and Marta Okoye, Orla's lawyer. Lucas is acting for the person who wants to buy the lodge.
Mr Bell, the caretaker, warns everyone that a great storm is coming. High tide is at six, and after that the causeway will be under the sea for a day or more.
Alone in the study, Ines studies The Grey Heron under a lamp. The varnish looks too fresh for an old painting, but she cannot be sure, and she decides to check it in the morning.
At six the storm arrives with a roar, and the sea covers the causeway. Ines lifts the telephone in the hall, but the line is dead, and her mobile has no signal.
At dinner Orla announces that she will sell the lodge and all of its paintings on Monday. Felix jumps to his feet and says that she is throwing away the family's home.
At a quarter to nine Orla stands up and says that she will fetch a special bottle from the cellar for a toast. She takes a key from a hook and goes out through the kitchen passage.
While Mrs Bright brings in the main course, Lucas says he must wash his hands and leaves the table. Hugh begins a long, nervous speech about the cost of keeping an old building.
At five past nine the lights go out with a bang, and the guests cry out in the dark. A minute later Lucas comes back into the room holding a candle, and he sits down again.
By half past nine Orla still has not come back from the cellar. Ines takes a candle, and Mr Bell, who has come back from the generator, goes with her to look.
At the end of the passage they find the cellar door shut with a bolt on the outside. When Mr Bell slides it back and opens the door, Orla is lying at the bottom of the steps.
Dr Priya hurries down and kneels beside Orla, but she can do nothing. Orla is dead, and the glass of her wristwatch is cracked, with the hands stopped at eight fifty-eight.
Everyone says that Orla must have fallen in the dark. Ines points out that the lights were still on at eight fifty-eight, and that Orla could not have bolted the cellar door from inside.
Ines tells the guests that she once worked with the police, and that someone in the house must be the killer. With the sea road closed, she says, they must find the truth themselves.
Mr Bell goes down to the little harbour with a lantern and comes back soaked. His boat, the only one on the island, has been smashed to pieces against the rocks by the waves.
One by one Ines asks the guests where they were at eight fifty-eight. They all say that they were sitting at the dining table, though no one can swear that nobody left it.
During the night Ines hears a noise and goes to the study. She finds Felix with a torch, opening every drawer in the desk, and he hurries away without a word.
On Saturday morning the storm is still blowing. Felix admits that he was looking for his aunt's new will, because he owes a great deal of money and hoped she would help him.
Marta Okoye quietly tells Ines what is in the new will. The lodge's money is to go to the island's lifeboat, and Felix will receive only a small gift.
Ines examines the account books with Hugh, who becomes very pale. At last he admits that he has been borrowing from Orla's money, but he swears that he planned to repay it.
Ines asks Gideon Frost to look at The Grey Heron. He stares at it for a long time and then says that it is not his painting, because the real one has a tiny white fleck in the bird's eye.
Ines understands at once that the painting in the study is a copy, and that the real Grey Heron has been stolen. It is worth a fortune, and a thief might kill to keep his secret.
Mrs Bright tells Ines something important. When Lucas returned to the dining room that night, he came from the kitchen passage, and his sleeve smelt of the cold, damp cellar.
Ines asks Lucas where he went when he left the table. He smiles and says that he went to the cloakroom, but his story does not fit what the cook has seen.
In the cellar by daylight, Ines finds a large gold frame hidden under a sheet. It is empty, and it carries a label that says Reyes Fine Art.

Ines understands what happened. Orla found the empty frame in the cellar and so learned about the theft, and the thief killed her; and with the sea road closed, he cannot have taken the painting away.
Ines and Mr Bell search every bedroom in the lodge, looking under beds and in cupboards. They find nothing, and Lucas watches them with a polite smile from the stairs.
In the afternoon Tamsin Reed whispers to Ines in the hall. Very early that morning, she says, she saw Lucas standing close to the grandfather clock, and its door was open.
Tamsin is too curious to wait. While the others are in the lounge, she decides to look inside the clock herself, though Ines has asked her not to go alone.
Ines, Mr Bell and Felix hurry through the house and soon hear a faint banging from the kitchen. It comes from the cold store, where the door has been wedged shut with a heavy chair.
Tamsin is found, cold and frightened, but unhurt. She says that she saw a long tube in the clock case before someone pushed her into the cold store and shut the door.
Ines hurries to the hall and opens the door of the clock case. The long tube that Tamsin found has gone, and the thief has taken it somewhere else.
Ines studies the tide table that hangs by Mr Bell's door and works out that the causeway will be free of water at twenty to five on Sunday morning. That will be the thief's moment.
Ines tells Mr Bell, Felix and Dr Priya what she thinks. They agree to help her, and Felix, ashamed of his behaviour, is the most willing of them all.
Ines sits in the dark kitchen with a blanket round her shoulders and watches the back door. The wind is dropping, and the sound of the sea is no longer so wild.
At three in the morning a soft footstep sounds in the passage. Lucas creeps through the kitchen in a long coat, opens the back door very gently and goes out into the dark.
Ines and Mr Bell follow Lucas down to the little harbour. He goes into the boathouse and comes out with a long tube, which he took from the broken boat.
The storm has passed, and a few stars are shining. At the edge of the water, the causeway begins to show, wet and shining in the starlight, as the tide falls away.
Lucas is just starting onto the causeway when Ines steps out of the dark behind him with a lantern. She calls his name in a clear, calm voice, and he stops.
Lucas turns and runs along the causeway. But Felix and Mr Bell have been waiting at the other end, and they step out of the dark and block his way.
Lucas sits down on the wet stones and tells them everything. He stole the real painting for a rich buyer abroad, and Orla found the frame in the cellar and faced him.
Ines opens the tube as the sky grows pale and unrolls the canvas on a dry stone. It is the real Grey Heron, and Gideon Frost, who has come down, points proudly to the white fleck in its eye.
At seven o'clock two police officers drive across the freshly opened causeway. Ines gives them her notebook and the tube, and they take Lucas Reyes away.
At breakfast the guests are subdued but relieved. Hugh promises to give back every penny he borrowed, and Felix quietly says that he is sorry for the way he spoke to his aunt.
In the afternoon Ines leaves Tern Rock, walking across the dry causeway in bright sunshine. The lodge will go to the lifeboat as Orla wished, and The Grey Heron will hang there again.
C1C2: On Friday afternoon, Mr Bell drove Ines Calloway across the stone causeway to Tern Rock Island in a battered old car that rattled over every wave-worn slab. The tide was out, and the wet sand shone like pewter on either side, but a bank of dark cloud was already piling up above the horizon. Ines, who disliked surprises, wondered whether the sea road would still be there on Sunday.

At the door of the old stone lodge stood Orla Venn, its owner, leaning on a silver-topped stick and smiling as though she had been expecting trouble and welcomed it. She was seventy years old, small and upright, with white hair and a pair of bright, quick eyes that missed nothing. Ines liked her at once, which was rarely a good sign for a woman in her profession.

Orla drew Ines into a quiet corner and explained, in a low voice, that she was about to sell the lodge and every painting in it. She had hired Ines to inspect the collection for the insurers, she said, and she wished to hear the truth about every canvas, however unwelcome it might be. Ines, noting the unusual stress on the word truth, promised that she would look closely.

Orla led her across the hall, past a tall grandfather clock whose slow ticking filled the stone passages, and into a small study lined with books. Above the fireplace hung the lodge's greatest treasure, The Grey Heron, a painting of a lone bird standing in the shallows at dawn, its reflection trembling in the water. It was, Orla declared, worth more than the whole island put together.

In the lounge, Ines was introduced to Felix Venn, Orla's nephew, a handsome man in a bright jacket whose easy laugh was just a little too ready. Beside him sat Hugh Marlowe, her accountant, a grey, stooping figure who kept glancing at his watch and stirring his tea long after it had gone cold. Neither of them, she noticed, looked entirely comfortable in the other's company.

Dr Priya Nair, Orla's physician and oldest friend, greeted her with a calm handshake and a smile that suggested nothing could ever alarm her. In the armchair beside the fire, an elderly man with wild white hair complained about the weather, the sandwiches and the modern world, and Ines learned that he was Gideon Frost, the painter of The Grey Heron. He seemed to have been grumbling for decades, and rather to enjoy it.

The last three guests were Lucas Reyes, a smooth, well-dressed art dealer who represented the buyer, Tamsin Reed, a young journalist with a notebook, and Marta Okoye, the lawyer, who said little and watched everything. Lucas shook hands with a warmth that Ines noticed did not quite reach his eyes. Eight guests in all, she counted, and the sea road was growing narrower by the hour.

Mr Bell, the caretaker and boatman, stood at the lounge window and announced in his flat, steady voice that a proper storm was coming up the coast. High tide at six would cover the causeway completely, he said, and with the wind in this direction it might stay covered for most of two days. The telephone, he added, had a habit of failing whenever the weather turned.

Alone in the study, Ines held a lamp close to The Grey Heron and studied the surface with the patient eye of her trade. The varnish seemed oddly bright and fresh for a painting supposedly thirty years old, though she told herself that the lamp might be to blame and that she should look again by daylight. She made a small note in her book and said nothing to anyone.

The storm broke at six with a roar of wind and rain, and from the hall window Ines watched the sea sweep over the causeway until no trace of it remained. When she lifted the telephone to call her office, she heard only a hollow silence, and her mobile showed not a single bar of signal. They were alone on the island, eight guests, a host and two members of staff.

At dinner, Orla rose and informed her guests, with a calm that silenced the room, that she would sell the lodge and its paintings on Monday. Felix leapt to his feet, white with anger, and accused her of squandering the family's home for the sake of some foolish whim. Orla looked at him with quiet sorrow and told him to sit down and finish his soup.

At a quarter to nine, Orla announced that the occasion called for something better than the lodge's ordinary wine, and that she would bring up a special bottle from the cellar herself. She took a key from a hook by the door and walked out along the kitchen passage, her stick tapping on the stone floor. The guests heard the sound grow fainter and then stop.

While Mrs Bright carried in the main course, Lucas Reyes murmured that he must wash his hands and slipped out of the dining room into the hall. Hugh Marlowe immediately launched into a long and nervous speech about the cost of keeping an old building, and few of the guests noticed the empty chair. Ines, glancing at the clock on the wall, saw that it was ten minutes to nine.

At five past nine, the electric lights died with a soft bang, and the dining room fell into a darkness filled with startled cries and the clatter of dropped forks. A minute or two later Lucas walked in from the hall carrying a lit candle, apologised for the confusion, and resumed his seat as if nothing had happened. Mr Bell hurried off to look at the old generator.

By half past nine, Orla had been gone for three-quarters of an hour, and a small, cold feeling of unease settled in Ines's stomach. She took a candle from the table, and Mr Bell, who had just returned from the generator shed with oil on his hands, offered to go with her. They walked together along the dark kitchen passage.

At the end of the passage stood the cellar door, shut fast, with an iron bolt on its outer side pushed firmly across. Mr Bell drew it back and swung the door open, and in the trembling light of the candle they saw Orla lying at the bottom of the stone steps, motionless, her stick beside her. The silence in the cellar seemed to press on their ears.

Dr Priya Nair hurried down the steps, knelt beside the old woman, and after a moment's careful examination looked up and said quietly that nothing could be done. Orla had struck her head on the stone floor, she explained, and she must have died almost at once. Ines, leaning close with the candle, saw that the glass of Orla's wristwatch was cracked and that its hands had stopped at eight fifty-eight.

Several guests murmured that the poor woman had simply fallen in the dark, but Ines shook her head and reminded them that the lights had not failed until five past nine. Her watch had stopped three minutes before that, she said, and in any case a woman at the bottom of the cellar steps could not have bolted the door on the outside. Someone had shut Orla in, and someone had left her there.

Back in the lounge, Ines told the frightened guests that she had worked beside the police for years and that she could not pretend to believe in an accident. The sea road was closed and the telephone dead, she said, and until help arrived someone in this room might well be a killer. Nobody answered her, but Hugh drew his chair a little closer to the fire.

Mr Bell took a lantern down to the little harbour to check the island's only boat, and he returned twenty minutes later drenched and grim. The vessel had been hurled against the rocks by the waves and broken into splinters, he said, so nobody would be leaving the island tonight by sea. The storm, Ines reflected, had imprisoned the guilty and the innocent together.

One by one, Ines questioned the guests about their movements, and one by one they told her that they had been sitting at the dining table when Orla died. It was a perfectly reasonable answer, but she soon discovered that nobody could swear that everyone else had remained in his chair throughout the meal. Mrs Bright was fetching dishes, Mr Bell was at the generator, and the candle-lit gloom had been thick.

Unable to sleep, Ines crept downstairs in the small hours, drawn by a faint scraping sound, and found the study door ajar. Inside, a torch beam danced over the papers on the desk, and Felix Venn knelt amid a heap of open drawers, searching like a man possessed. He saw her, muttered something she could not catch, and brushed past her into the dark.

On Saturday morning, with the wind still howling round the chimneys, Felix admitted that he had been searching for his aunt's new will in the hope of learning what she had left him. He owed a great deal of money to some unpleasant people, he confessed, and her decision to sell had filled him with panic. He swore on his mother's memory that he had never gone near the cellar.

In a quiet corner of the library, Marta Okoye admitted that she knew the contents of Orla's new will and felt that the matter could not now be kept secret. The lodge and its money, she said, were to go to the island's lifeboat, and Felix would receive no more than a small gift to remember his aunt by. Felix, Ines realised, had not known this, and so the will gave him no reason to hurry his aunt's death.

When Ines asked to see the accounts, Hugh Marlowe turned the colour of old paper and finally confessed that he had been borrowing small sums from Orla's money for two years. He had always intended to repay every penny, he insisted, and the sale would have uncovered it, but he had never in his life raised his hand against anyone. Mrs Bright, passing with a tray, confirmed that he had not left his chair all evening.

Ines asked the old painter to look carefully at The Grey Heron, and for a long minute he stared at it in silence, his nose almost touching the canvas. Then he straightened up, red in the face, and declared that this was not his picture, because the real bird had a tiny fleck of white in its eye which he had put there for luck and had never told anyone about. This heron's eye was perfectly dark.

Ines understood in a flash that the heron on the study wall was a clever copy, and that the original, worth more than the lodge itself, had been quietly removed. A man who had stolen so valuable a painting would be desperate to prevent anyone from examining it before the sale, and a woman who had discovered the swap might be a danger to him. It was a motive far stronger than anything Felix or Hugh possessed.

Mrs Bright, wiping her hands on her apron, told Ines in an undertone that the gentleman in the pale suit had come back to the dining room along the kitchen passage on Friday night. She remembered it clearly because his sleeve had been covered in dust and had smelt of the cold, damp cellar, although he had claimed to have been at the cloakroom. The cloakroom was at the front of the house, and the passage ran to the back.

When Ines asked Lucas Reyes where he had been at a quarter to nine, he smiled in his easy way and answered that he had visited the cloakroom to wash his hands. His manner was smooth, and his explanation might have convinced anyone who had not heard the cook, but Ines noticed that his shoes were still dusty and that he kept turning the signet ring on his finger. She thanked him politely and let him go.

In the cellar, by the grey light of a small high window, Ines found a tall shape draped in a dusty sheet and pulled the cloth aside. Underneath stood a magnificent gilded frame with nothing in it, and on its back was fixed a neat printed label bearing the words Reyes Fine Art. It was exactly the shape and size of the frame in the study that now held the false heron.

The pieces of the puzzle fell neatly into place in Ines's mind: Orla had gone down for wine, discovered the empty frame, and understood in a single terrible moment what had been done to her. The thief had followed her, struck her down, and bolted the door, and since the sea road was closed, the stolen canvas must still be somewhere on the island. It could be rolled up small, and a clever man could hide it almost anywhere.

With Mr Bell's help, Ines searched every bedroom in the lodge, looking beneath beds, inside wardrobes and behind curtains, while the guests grumbled and protested. The long, narrow roll of canvas that she sought was nowhere to be found, and Lucas Reyes watched from the top of the stairs with a polite and unreadable smile. By the end of the morning, Ines was beginning to feel that she was being outwitted.

In the afternoon Tamsin Reed drew Ines aside and whispered that she had been awake at dawn and had seen Lucas Reyes standing beside the grandfather clock in the hall. The door of the clock case had been open, she said, and he had been feeling about inside it as though looking for something he had hidden there. She had thought nothing of it until Ines began asking about the missing painting.

Tamsin Reed, who had a journalist's restless curiosity and little patience, decided that she would not wait for Ines to look inside the clock. While the others drank tea in the lounge and the storm roared against the windows, she crept out into the hall alone, although Ines had specially begged her to stay in the company of others. The long case ticked solemnly as she approached.

Ines, Felix and Mr Bell hurried through the lodge calling Tamsin's name, until at last they heard a faint, steady banging from the kitchen. It came from the cold store, a heavy-walled room used for meat and dairy, whose door had been wedged shut with the back of a heavy chair. Felix tore the chair away and Mr Bell dragged the door open.

They found Tamsin shivering on the stone floor, her lips blue with cold, and Mr Bell wrapped her in a blanket and carried her to the stove. Between sips of hot tea she explained that she had found a long cardboard tube inside the clock, and that the next moment a hand had pushed her violently through the cold store door. She had not seen the face, she said, but she had smelt expensive soap.

Ines hurried back to the hall and flung open the long door of the grandfather clock, and found nothing inside but the dusty weights and the swinging pendulum. The tube had gone, and its removal showed that the thief was neither stupid nor idle, and that he was still within a few feet of them somewhere in the lodge. Lucas Reyes, when he strolled in a little later, looked entirely innocent.

On the wall of Mr Bell's cottage hung the tide table, and Ines read it slowly, working out that the storm was now falling and that the causeway would emerge from the sea at twenty minutes to five on Sunday morning. A thief who could not escape by water would surely wait for the sand to appear and then cross it in the darkness, long before any police arrived. She knew then exactly when and where she must be.

She told her plan to Mr Bell, Felix and Dr Priya in a whisper, and each of them promised to help, though she took care to say nothing in the presence of the others. Felix, who was still ashamed of his midnight search of the study, volunteered with such passion that she almost smiled. The thief would be allowed to feel safe, she said, until the moment he stepped out into the night.

Ines sat in the dark kitchen with a blanket round her shoulders, her eyes fixed on the back door, and listened as the wind slowly lost its fury. The sea, too, seemed to be easing, and the rain had faded to a thin patter against the glass, so that the old lodge creaked and settled like a ship in calmer water. She had never known a night pass so slowly.

At three in the morning, the soft tread of a stockinged foot sounded in the passage, and a tall figure in a long coat slipped silently into the kitchen. Lucas Reyes crossed the floor without a glance at the corner where Ines sat motionless in the shadows, drew back the bolt of the back door, and stepped into the night. She counted to thirty and then followed.

Ines and Mr Bell followed at a safe distance, keeping to the shadow of the wall as Lucas strode down the rocky path to the little harbour. He vanished into the boathouse, and a minute later emerged with a long cardboard tube, which he had evidently hidden inside the splintered hull of Mr Bell's wrecked boat. He tucked it under his coat and turned towards the causeway.

The clouds had been torn apart by the dying wind, and a scatter of stars shone above the island as the sea drew back from the causeway. Wet stone and pale sand gleamed in the starlight, and a narrow pathway of dry land crept slowly out across the water towards the mainland. It was twenty minutes to five, exactly as the tide table had promised.

Lucas had taken barely a dozen steps along the glistening causeway when Ines stepped out of the darkness behind him, raised her lantern and called his name in a clear and steady voice. He stopped dead, and for a long moment the only sound was the soft hiss of the retreating tide. Then he turned slowly, with the cardboard tube still clutched against his chest.

For an instant Lucas stood quite still, and then he wheeled round and began to run along the slippery stones, his coat flapping behind him. He had not gone fifty yards when two dark shapes rose out of the shadows ahead, and Felix and Mr Bell, who had walked round the shore to wait for him, stood side by side across the road. There was nowhere left for him to run.

Lucas Reyes sank onto a wet slab of stone and, with a weary, hollow voice, told them everything. He had stolen The Grey Heron to sell to a rich collector abroad, he said, and Orla had found its empty frame in the cellar and challenged him, so that in a moment of panic he had pushed her away. He had never meant her to fall, he insisted, but he had bolted the door anyway.

As the sky turned pale with dawn, Ines opened the tube with careful fingers and unrolled the canvas upon a dry slab of stone, and there, in all its quiet beauty, lay The Grey Heron. Gideon Frost, who had hobbled down to the shore on his stick, bent over it and pointed with a trembling finger to the tiny white fleck gleaming in the bird's eye. His grumbling, for once, had completely vanished.

At seven o'clock, two police officers in yellow coats picked their way across the dripping causeway, summoned at last by the first working signal of the morning. Ines handed them her notebook, the tube and the empty gilded frame from the cellar, and Lucas Reyes, pale and silent, was led away across the glittering sand. The island was finally free.

At breakfast the guests sat round the long table in a weary, subdued silence, glad of the sunshine pouring through the windows. Hugh Marlowe gravely promised Marta that he would repay every borrowed penny, and Felix, with a broken voice, said that he regretted every angry word he had spoken to his aunt. Mrs Bright, for the first time that weekend, allowed herself a small smile.

That afternoon, Ines walked back across the causeway in bright sunshine, with the sea glittering quietly on either side and the lodge growing small behind her. Orla's wishes would be carried out, Marta had promised, so that the lodge would help the lifeboat that saved sailors and The Grey Heron would hang once more over the study fire. Ines had never known a house so quiet and so clear after a storm.
